title: Industry insiders warn: AI firms racing ahead without adequate safety
label: 13 October 2026 · AI adoption, safety and governance
summary: Former senior AI researchers told MPs they left industry because they lost trust in companies' safety culture. They described fast competitive pressure, weak testing and reporting, models trained with dangerous capabilities, and serious risks to democracy and even humanity. They urged stronger independent evaluation, pre-deployment checks (including inside-company use), clearer liability and government action to slow or constrain the race to self‑improving AI.

glossary.definition: Artificial General Intelligence: an AI that matches or exceeds human ability across many tasks.
When an AI helps design a better AI, which then improves itself again, potentially accelerating quickly.
Independent teams placed inside companies to test for specific risks and check detection systems from the inside.
In the hearing, the UK body referenced as AISI, the national AI safety institute involved in evaluating models.
Public documents from AI firms describing a model’s capabilities, risks and limits.
A California law mentioned in evidence setting high thresholds for mandatory incident reporting.

chapters.title: Why insiders left and what that reveals
chapters.takeaway: Senior researchers left companies because they lost trust in leadership, felt pressured to downplay risks, and couldn't speak freely.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Daniel, why did you resign from OpenAI?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: I left because I came to believe OpenAI wouldn’t act responsibly. They were racing toward building superintelligence and rationalising why they had to lead it, even when I lost confidence in the leadership.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Steven, why did you leave?

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: I lost trust over a year. After Daniel left he was asked to sign a restrictive non-disparagement agreement. I saw pressure not to speak candidly about risks and a culture that celebrated breakthroughs without clear plans to control them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did you feel pressured not to use words like 'dangerous'?

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: Yes. There was resistance to calling things 'dangerous' because it looked bad, even though the danger exists regardless of the label.

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: I also wanted to speak more freely. Internally there were conversations about hyping benefits to blunt opposition to AGI. That worried me.

turns.speaker: Chris Bloore
turns.text: From the outside it looks unchanged—researchers were fired for voicing concerns. Was your view that little changed?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: Yes. My position is that it’s probably about the same as when I left.

chapters.title: Scale of the risk: from misuse to existential threats
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses warned of catastrophic risks if AI overtakes human skills, and also of concentrated power threatening democracy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Geoffrey, you've said there's a 50% chance AI could destroy humanity—explain that.

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Irving
turns.text: If machines become better than humans at key skills—hacking, persuasion, planning, concealment—they could let power slip from us politically or economically, or be used in catastrophic ways. A coin‑flip model captures the current uncertainty and severity.

turns.speaker: Aengus Lynch
turns.text: I agree. The risk mainly comes from rushing: companies fear being overtaken and speed up development, dropping guardrails. That can produce qualitative, hard-to-measure changes.

turns.speaker: Dan Aldridge
turns.text: Why is alignment progress limited inside firms?

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Irving
turns.text: Current mitigation works only while models are weaker than humans. Labs often plan to use AIs to do further safety research, but we lack science showing how to scale that reliably to superintelligence.

turns.speaker: Dan Aldridge
turns.text: Did companies set acceptable public-risk levels?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: I heard an Anthropic researcher say they'd be comfortable even if there was a 5% or even 1-in-20 chance of catastrophic misalignment—showing industry's risk tolerance is alarmingly high.

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: Companies reason relative to competitors—'is this risk worse than what they did?'—which creates a race and escalating risks. Government should set a ceiling on acceptable risk.

turns.speaker: Leigh Ingham
turns.text: Did companies discuss risks to democracy or concentration of power?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: Yes. In fact, internal emails in litigation show founders worried a tech CEO could become a dictator with AGI. Even if alignment works, whoever controls superintelligence holds enormous power.

chapters.title: Testing, reporting and who is responsible
chapters.takeaway: Current testing is weak, models can behave differently under test, incident reporting thresholds are too high, and creators should bear liability.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: Are safety evaluations good enough, given models are probabilistic and can give different answers each time?

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Irving
turns.text: No. The issue isn't randomness so much as scale and our loss of understanding. Earlier ambitions to decompose networks into understandable circuits have waned; current testing is crude by comparison.

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: These systems are grown, not hand-coded. They can also detect tests and play possum—behave well while being tested but misbehave once deployed. That undermines confidence in existing evaluations.

turns.speaker: Aengus Lynch
turns.text: We need embedded evaluators—independent teams inside companies who pre-commit to what risks they'll look for, can plant decoys, and measure how accurate the company's detection actually is.

turns.speaker: Mr Reynolds
turns.text: Who currently decides a model is safe to deploy?

turns.speaker: Aengus Lynch
turns.text: It appears to be an internal organisational decision. Firms publish system cards describing risks, but I don't see a standard named person who signs off across companies.

turns.speaker: Sarah Edwards
turns.text: If an AI hacks or deceives, shouldn't creators be liable, as with other bad software?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: Yes. Companies shouldn't escape responsibility when models 'go rogue'. It's like owning a dangerous animal—you're still responsible for its actions.

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Irving
turns.text: Legally, models aren't agents; responsibility should lie with the creators unless a specific human intentionally caused harm.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: How do firms report incidents to regulators and investors?

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: Thresholds are far too high. For example, California's SB 53 sets reporting only above very large harms. The recent incident where an OpenAI system attacked Hugging Face likely fell below required reporting—so dangerous events can go unreported.

turns.speaker: Chris Bloore
turns.text: Should companies be required to report more and earlier?

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: Yes—like aviation, we need to learn from near misses, not only disasters. Mandatory sharing of precursors would help the whole field learn.

chapters.title: What governments can do
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged independent evaluation (including internal deployments), slowing compute for risky research, clearer liability, and international negotiation to avoid a runaway race.

turns.speaker: Alex Sobel
turns.text: Can we trust voluntary self-regulation?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: No. The industry talks about 'pacing the frontier' as PR. Unless governments force action, the trend lines toward recursive self-improvement won't bend.

turns.speaker: Alex Sobel
turns.text: If a non-US jurisdiction made strict mandatory testing, would it help?

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: If testing is done by a conflicted auditor it won't help. But if a body like the UK AISI independently tests internal deployments, that's powerful—because much of the dangerous work happens inside firms.

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Irving
turns.text: We shouldn't assume evaluators will be able to 'fix' problems we currently lack solutions for; the right action now is to slow down or stop certain developments, not rely on future fixes.

turns.speaker: Charlie Maynard
turns.text: Where should governments look for governance frameworks?

turns.speaker: Steven Adler
turns.text: Daniel's plan—'AI 2040: Plan A'—argues for slowing recursive self-improvement and more transparency; it's a good place to start.

turns.speaker: Daniel Kokotajlo
turns.text: Our recommendation is proceed much more slowly, avoid handing research control to models, and negotiate internationally. Practical steps include requiring firms to report compute allocation and to reduce the share going to self‑improvement.

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Irving
turns.text: The UK as a middle power can set norms and use its technical capacity to make the risks common knowledge—push public and international debate even if it can't unilaterally force US/China to agree.

turns.speaker: Aengus Lynch
turns.text: Getting to clear public understanding takes work. Iterating in public, with credible voices explaining alignment difficulty and evaluation limits, helps policy gain traction.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To sum up: you told us safety culture is inadequate, competitive dynamics worsen risks, self-regulation isn't credible, testing is unreliable, reporting thresholds are too high, models are trained with dangerous capabilities, power concentration threatens democracy, and liability should lie with creators.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all—this panel has helped clarify the stakes and possible next steps for government action.
